links.outcome: Fairness metrics and accuracy before vs after bias mitigation (adversarial debiasing, BPA, equalised odds)
links.effect: Disparate impact rose from 0.80 to 0.95 and equal opportunity difference fell from 0.20 to 0.05. BPA cut FPR for males 0.0059 to 0.0033 and females 0.0096 to 0.0064. Overall accuracy effect after mitigation not clearly reported.
links.quote: For example, disparate impact increased from 0.80 to 0.95, and equal opportunity difference decreased from 0.20 to 0.05, demonstrating significant reductions in demographic bias.

links.outcome: Class-level and gender-level performance gaps hidden behind aggregate metrics
links.effect: YOLO overall mAP 0.88, but the 'abnormal' class had precision 78% and recall 72% (28% miss rate) vs 94% recall for 'serious'. Gender mean outcome differences were also observed.
links.quote: The mean average precision (mAP) of 0.88 underscores an overall solid performance, but the lower precision and recall for the “abnormal” class reveal a masked bias that could exacerbate health disparities.

links.outcome: Model robustness to input noise perturbation
links.effect: ResNet18 prediction accuracy dropped 29.7% (111 to 78 correct) as noise increased from 0.01 to 0.05, while YOLO perturbation sensitivity was 0.0.
links.quote: The ResNet’s significant 29.7% prediction accuracy drop (111 to 78) under increased noise conditions (0.01 to 0.05) particularly threatens the project’s aim of fair diagnostics across different healthcare settings, potentially discriminating against facilities with limited resources or older equipment.

unlisted_practices: Use of SCIR/SIR compartmental models to simulate population-level effects of algorithmic bias

links.effect: SCIR recovery rate was 1.38 vs SIR 0.83, with a -10% transmission bias impact.
links.quote: The SCIR model outperformed the SIR model (recovery rate: 1.38 vs 0.83) with a -10% transmission bias impact.

links.effect: Recall differed by 22% between serious (94%) and abnormal (72%) cases.
links.quote: This 22% discrepancy in the recall between “serious” (94%) and “abnormal” (72%) cases poses a critical challenge as early-stage abnormalities often require timely intervention but remain underdetected.

links.effect: Disparate impact improved 0.80 to 0.95; equal opportunity difference fell 0.20 to 0.05; false favourable rates fell for males and females.
links.quote: Bias mitigation improved disparate impact (0.80 to 0.95), reduced equal opportunity difference (0.20 to 0.05), and decreased false favourable rates for males (0.0059 to 0.0033) and females (0.0096 to 0.0064) through balanced probability adjustment.

screen.practice: fairness-aware bias mitigation (debiasing, equalised odds post-processing)
screen.reason: The study empirically tests and compares bias mitigation and post-processing fairness methods (adversarial debiasing, Fairlearn, equalized odds post-processing) on cardiovascular imaging/risk prediction models to measure reduction in demographic bias metrics.
